transcript:
[00:00:00] Sara (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I'm Sara, AE at Redwood; with me is Devon and Liam from our SE team. Quick agenda: understand your workload, budget, and what success looks like.
[00:00:22] Maya (Inkwell): Thanks. We're excited. Quick context: we're adding multi-doc summarization and a routing layer to our analytics UX. Estimated 120k active users, roughly 3M tokens/day initially, spiking to 15M in peak. Main ask: how do we keep per-interaction cost predictable while hitting <300ms p95? Budget cap: $12k/mo for inference in phase 1.
[00:01:05] Devon (Redwood SE): Okay that's great, appreciate the numbers. A few clarifying Qs: are those 3M tokens mostly in short chat-like requests or long-context summarize jobs? And do you have an SLA requirement for all endpoints or just interactive ones?
[00:01:25] Andre (Inkwell): Mix — ~70% short (50-150 tokens), 30% long (1k-3k) for nightly batches. Interactive endpoints need the 300ms p95; nightly can be minutes.
[00:01:44] Sara (Redwood): Perfect. So for economics we usually show unit-cost scenarios: hosted per-token, dedicated reserved capacity amortized, and private (VPC/on-prem) where infra cost + ops matter. We'll also show how batching, KV cache and prefix caching change per-token cost.
[00:02:10] Maya: Can you give a rough order of magnitude now? Ballpark hosted cost for our mix?
[00:02:18] Liam (Redwood SE): Rough ballpark: hosted generation for mixed short/long could be ~$0.0008 - $0.0025 per token depending on model size and whether streaming VS chunked outputs. But that's very rough — quantization and efficient kernels bring it down.
[00:02:40] Priya (Inkwell): That's... higher than our expectation. At $0.0025, 3M tokens is $7.5k, but spikes to 15M would be 37.5k — over budget.
[00:02:58] Devon: Right, that's where dedicated and caching help. With a dedicated reserved pool you amortize GPU cost; depending on utilization you can get to ~$0.0003 - $0.0007 per token. Add batching and prefix caching, night batches for long-context, you can push effective unit to the 0.0002 range for steady state.
[00:03:20] Maya: Can you explain prefix caching — is that the same as KV cache? We've heard both terms.
[00:03:30] Liam: Related but different. KV cache is per-request attention state (we retain it across streaming); prefix or prefix-KV caching stores repeated prompt prefixes or static context so we don't recompute first N tokens. So if your summarization has a fixed system prompt or repeated legal disclaimers, we can cache those. For LLMs with long context this reduces token compute.
[00:04:02] Andre: Any gotchas? Does caching change output determinism or freshness?
[00:04:10] Devon: It can. If you cache prefixes you need eviction strategies for personalization; also cached outputs may slightly change latency profile. For freshness we recommend TTLs or per-user version keys. We'll share sample configs in the runbook.
[00:04:34] Priya: Ok but how much of a chunk are we actually saving? 70%? 20%?
[00:04:40] Liam: It depends. For chat flows with 70% short messages, prefix caching might save 10-30% of compute; for flows with repeated system prompt it could be 40-60%. We usually model conservative 20% savings initially.
[00:05:05] Maya: What about batching? Our interactive requirement seems to push against batching.
[00:05:11] Devon: Correct. Batching reduces per-token cost by increasing GPU utilization but adds latency. Redwood's runtime supports dynamic batching with latency SLOs — you can cap batch windows to keep p95 under target. For sub-300ms interactive you may only accept micro-batches or single-request low-latency paths, and push long jobs into dedicated background workers.
[00:05:40] Maya: Let's talk about private VPC — we have some regulated clients requiring data residency and KMS control. What are tradeoffs?
[00:05:50] Sara: Private gives control (customer-managed VPC, KMS/HSM integration). Cost is higher because you're managing infra and ops or paying for an on-prem license. Typical breakdown: hosted lowest friction but limited residency guarantees; dedicated gives predictable throughput and isolation; private has the highest fixed cost but gives compliance posture. We'll show expected TCO vs scale.
[00:06:18] Andre: For private, what's the typical lead time and who handles model updates?
[00:06:24] Liam: Lead time depends on networking and security review (usually 4-8 weeks). Model updates can be automated through our control plane or shipped as artifacts; we support canary rollouts and pinned versions. There was a note in transcript earlier incorrectly saying 'KV cash' which should be KV cache —sorry for the auto transcript funnyness.
[00:06:48] Priya: From FinOps perspective we care about unit economics and predictability. Can you model a committed spend vs variable? Incentives and discounts?
[00:06:56] Devon: Yes. Dedicated reserved capacity uses committed monthly/annual contracts with step-down per-token rates. We usually present three scenarios: pay-as-you-go hosted, monthly committed dedicated, and self-managed private. We'll include break-even points given utilization.
[00:07:20] Maya: If we have bursts, do you support bursting on top of dedicated?
[00:07:24] Sara: Yes — dedicated pools can be configured with burst capacity or fallback to hosted variants. There's also policy-based routing: route critical low-latency traffic to reserved nodes and less-critical to cheaper fallback.
[00:07:40] Andre: How do you handle long-context summarization where we hit 3k tokens — do we chunk?
[00:07:46] Liam: We recommend chunking with overlap for quality, combined with a reranker or extractive summary step to keep token costs down. Long batch jobs can run on cheaper nodes without strict latency constraints.
[00:08:10] Priya: Security: SOC2 and KMS — do you have SOC2 cert? We need audit logs per request level and SSO integration.
[00:08:17] Sara: Yes, Redwood has SOC2 Type II (we'll share the report under an NDA) and we have SAML/SSO + fine-grained RBAC. Audit logs and per-request metadata are available via our console and exported to your SIEM. We'll attach security docs.
[00:08:40] Maya: Any red flags for us? Things that usually blow budgets?
[00:08:45] Devon: Unbounded context windows and no batching or prefix caches. Also using a very large base model when a smaller tuned model matches quality will increase cost dramatically. We'll recommend a model sizing exercise.
[00:09:02] Maya: Can Redwood help with quantization or lower-precision kernels? We've read about 4-bit int8 etc.
[00:09:10] Liam: Yes, our runtime supports quantized weights and optimized kernels; quantization can reduce memory and accelerate throughput with small quality tradeoffs. We'll include expected perf impacts and quality checks in the evaluation.
[00:09:34] Andre: For the benchmark, what do you need from us?
[00:09:38] Devon: A representative sample of prompts and expected QPS distribution, latency SLO per endpoint, and a dataset for long-context summarization. Also credentialed access to a staging dataset for the run. Ideally a 48-72 hour window where traffic simulates peak and off-peak.
[00:09:58] Priya: We'll prepare that. Another question: do you expose token-level billing and attribution by endpoint? We need this for FinOps.
[00:10:06] Sara: Yes — Redwood Console has token-level breakdown by route/model, cost attribution, and you can tag tokens by project. We'll include screenshots in the docs.
[00:10:18] Maya: On fallback policies, if dedicated saturates do requests get dropped or routed to hosted?
[00:10:24] Devon: Routed to hosted fallback or configured to queue based on policy. There are options: fail-open to hosted, queue with backpressure, or return degraded responses. We can tailor for your SLA.
[00:10:40] Andre: Any perf numbers you can share for the models we might run?
[00:10:44] Liam: We'll attach a model profile, but example: for a 7B model on A100-like GPUs, you might get X tokens/sec in single-token latency mode vs Y tokens/sec with batching. (auto-transcript mistranscribed 'A100' as 'A-one-hundred' earlier). We'll send exact bench table.
[00:11:08] Maya: Ok this is helpful. Walk me through the immediate commercial options and what we'd sign up for to start a pilot.
[00:11:15] Sara: Pilot typically starts hosted for fastest time-to-value, with a short dedicated proof of concept if predictability required. We can do a 30-day pilot with committed committed credits — pilot pricing is flexible. For Private we usually require an enterprise engagement. We'll provide a pilot quote in the spreadsheet.
[00:11:38] Priya: For our budgeting round we need a clear 3-scenario cost for 3M, 7M, and 15M tokens/month with conservative caching and aggressive caching.
[00:11:49] Devon: We'll model those buckets and show break-even for dedicated vs hosted assuming utilization bands and effective per-token reductions for batching and caching.
[00:12:02] Maya: Great. Any outstanding security blockers?
[00:12:06] Sara: Not from our side — we'll supply SOC2, data handling, KMS docs. If you require in-country residency for model weights, that's a larger private engagement.
[00:12:20] Andre: Let's set the benchmark week. We prefer the week of July 6th.
[00:12:24] Sara: Noted. We'll follow up with calendar invites and the runbook.
